cards.text: Paul is writing to the believers in Rome, and he just said God did not reject His people Israel. A remnant was chosen by grace, and the others were hardened. Now Paul asks the big one: did they stumble so as to fall beyond recovery?

cards.question: Paul says Israel stumbled so badly that they fell beyond recovery.

cards.text: “Certainly not!” Two words, friend. ZERO wiggle room. But because of Israel's trespass, something has come to the Gentiles, the nations who aren't Israel.

cards.question: Because of Israel's trespass, what has come to the Gentiles?
Paul says salvation has come to the Gentiles to make Israel ___.

cards.text: Watch Paul now, baker. This man is about to do MATH: if Israel's trespass means riches for the world, and their failure means riches for the Gentiles, then what?

cards.question: What does Paul say Israel's fullness will bring?

cards.text: Then Paul talks straight to the Gentiles. He's the apostle to the Gentiles, and he magnifies his ministry, hoping to provoke his own people to jealousy.

cards.question: Paul hopes to provoke his own people to jealousy and ___ some of them.

cards.text: And Paul will NOT sit down. If their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, he asks, what will their acceptance be?

cards.question: Paul asks what Israel's acceptance will be. What does he call it?

cards.text: Then Paul pulls out a picture, and baker, it's DOUGH. Years I sat on a kitchen counter, and FINALLY a letter in the Bible talks my language.

cards.question: Paul says if the first part of the dough is holy, so is the ___ batch.
Right after the dough, Paul gives a tree picture: if the root is holy, the branches are not.

cards.text: Paul stays with that tree and talks to the Gentiles. If some branches have been broken off, and you, a wild olive shoot, have been grafted in among the others to share the olive root's nourishment, Paul has something to tell you.

cards.question: What does Paul tell the wild olive shoot not to do over the broken-off branches?
Paul reminds the grafted-in wild shoot that it supports the root.

cards.text: Paul even hears the comeback before it's said: “Branches were broken off so that I could be grafted in.” Paul agrees that's correct, and then he keeps talking, and friend, when somebody agrees with you and KEEPS talking, brace yourself.

cards.question: Paul says the natural branches were broken off because of ___, but you stand by ___.

cards.text: Then Paul says, “Do not be arrogant, but be afraid.” And he gives the reason, and it's about those natural branches.

cards.question: Paul says that if God did not spare the natural branches, He will surely spare the grafted-in ones.

cards.text: So Paul says take notice. There are two sides of God to see here, like flipping a cookie over, friend: you've got to check BOTH.

cards.question: Branches broken off, a wild shoot grafted in. Which two things about God does Paul tell the Gentiles to notice?
Paul says God shows severity to those who fell and kindness to the grafted-in Gentiles. On what condition?

answers.text: If they continue in His kindness
If they keep every single rule
If they stay far away from Israel

cards.text: Now Paul turns back to the branches that got broken off. Baker, a stamper who spent years in the back of a junk drawer is leaning WAY in for this part.

cards.question: Paul says the broken-off branches can never be grafted back in, even if they do not persist in unbelief.

cards.text: Paul's got one last move. If the Gentiles were cut from a wild olive tree and, contrary to nature, grafted into a cultivated one, then think how much more readily it can happen for the others.

cards.question: Paul says, How much more readily will these, the ___ branches, be grafted into their own olive tree!

findings.problem: The opening card states facts from outside the passage without references. It says Paul is writing to the believers in Rome (Romans 1:7), that God did not reject His people Israel (Romans 11:2), that a remnant was chosen by grace (Romans 11:5) and that the others were hardened (Romans 11:7). The card cites only Romans 11:11.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: This story card has four sentences: "Certainly not!", "Two words, friend.", "ZERO wiggle room." and the sentence about the Gentiles. Story cards after the opening card are limited to 1 to 2 sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The right answer stands out. "Life from the dead" sounds like Bible wording, and "A loss for the world" and "A pause for the world" sound flat and plainly go against the 'if this, then how much more' pattern the setup just showed.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: The card cites Romans 11:20 but also tells content from 11:21: that Paul's reason is about the natural branches. The phrase 'natural branches' first appears in 11:21.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: "His patience and anger" is a near-match for kindness and severity. Patience is close to kindness, and anger is close to severity, so a baker could argue it's right. "His silence and mercy" also overlaps, since mercy is close to kindness.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The right answer echoes "kindness" from the question itself, so it stands out. The wrong answers also differ in tone: "every single rule" is emphatic, and "stay far away from Israel" sounds off. Neither sounds like the right answer.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: No card tells the warning at the end of Romans 11:22: "Otherwise you also will be cut off." This is a key detail of the passage's argument, and it is left out.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: No card tells the reason Romans 11:23 gives: "for God is able to graft them in again." Card 12 asks only whether the branches can be grafted back in. God's ability to do it is the heart of the verse, and the baker never hears it.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: The answer "natural" is given away by earlier cards. Cards 5, 6 and 7 all call the broken-off branches "the natural branches." By card 14 the blank no longer tests anything.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.
